label: subject marker
meaning_en: The subject particle “이/가”: it marks the subject of a sentence, and in particular puts the focus on the subject itself: new information, the answer to “who/what”, or a described state. It also marks the complement of “되다” and “아니다”.
usage: After a consonant it is “이”, after a vowel “가”: “책이, 지수가”. Some pronouns change: “나 → 내가, 저 → 제가, 너 → 네가, 누구 → 누가”. It introduces new information (“옛날 옛적에 호랑이가 살았어요”), answers a question word (“누가 왔어요?”), and marks the subject of descriptions (“비가 와요”). With “좋다”, “싫다”, “필요하다” and “있다/없다” of possession, the thing wanted or had also takes “이/가” (“저는 한국어가 재미있어요”). Double subjects are common: “코끼리는 코가 길다”. Honorific subjects take “께서”.

examples.en: Jisu went to school.
Who opened this window?
It is raining.
I find Korean interesting.
This time I will do it.
An elephant's trunk is long.

compare.difference: “이/가” focuses on the subject: new information or an answer to “who”. “은/는” makes it the topic, with the known or contrasted thing.
“께서” is the honorific “이/가”: with the verb in “-시-”.

pitfalls.note: “나, 저, 너” change before “가”: “내가, 제가, 네가”.
New information (a new character) takes “이/가”, not “은/는”.
pitfalls.en: Once upon a time, a tiger lived.

topik_tip: Questions with “누가/무엇이” are answered with “이/가”: the answer is the subject in focus.

label: and; with
meaning_en: A particle that joins nouns (“A and B”) and marks a partner or comparison (“with, as”): “친구와 함께, 한국과 일본, 이것과 같다”. It is the written, neutral form of “하고” and “이랑”.
usage: After a consonant it is “과”, after a vowel “와”: “책과 연필, 사과와 배”. Listing: “N과 N”. Partner: with reciprocal verbs (“만나다, 싸우다, 결혼하다, 이야기하다, 헤어지다”) the partner takes “와/과” (“친구와 싸우다”). Comparison: “N과 같다/다르다/비슷하다”. “N과 함께” means “together with N”. It sounds written or formal, while speech prefers “하고/이랑”.

examples.en: I study Korean and English.
I watched a movie with a friend.
This outfit is different in color from that one.
Jisu quarreled with Minjun yesterday.
Korea and Japan are close neighbors.

compare.difference: “과/와” and “하고” are near-synonyms; “하고” is the neutral spoken form and attaches to any noun.
With verbs of talking, “와/과” means “with” (a conversation), “에게” means “to” (telling).

pitfalls.note: After a consonant the form is “과”.
pitfalls.en: Korea and Japan are close neighbors.

pitfalls.note: The partner of a reciprocal verb takes “와/과”, not “을/를”.

topik_tip: The partner of “만나다, 싸우다, 결혼하다” takes “와/과” (or “하고/이랑”), not “을/를”.

label: until, up to, even
meaning_en: A particle for the endpoint of a time or place range: “until, up to, as far as”. With a deadline verb it means “by”, and after a noun that is the last in a series it means “even”.
usage: It attaches to nouns of time and place: “열 시까지, 내일까지, 부산까지”. The pair “N부터 N까지” gives a range (“아홉 시부터 열 시까지”). With a continuing action it is “until” (“여섯 시까지 일해요”); with a one-time action such as “내다, 오다, 끝내다” it is a deadline, “by” (“내일까지 내세요”). In “너까지” it means “even you”. After a verb the ending form is “-ㄹ 때까지” (until the time when ...). It can be followed by other particles (“까지는, 까지도”).

examples.en: Today I work until six in the evening.
Submit your homework by tomorrow.

examples.ko: 집에서 학교까지 걸어서 이십 분 걸려요.
examples.en: It takes twenty minutes on foot from home to school.
It takes about three hours by train to Busan.
What am I supposed to do if even you do not believe me?

compare.difference: “에” marks a point in time; “까지” marks the end of a stretch.

pair.en: I go to bed at ten.

compare.difference: “부터” gives the start, “까지” the end; they often come in a pair.

pitfalls.note: After a verb, use “-ㄹ 때까지”, not “까지” alone.
pitfalls.en: I waited until my friend came.

topik_tip: “N까지” is “until” for a continuing action and “by” for a one-time deadline; both appear in TOPIK.

label: honorific subject
meaning_en: The honorific subject particle: it replaces “이/가” for a person to be respected (“선생님께서, 할아버지께서”). The verb takes the honorific “-시-”.
usage: It attaches to a person noun of higher status: “선생님께서, 부모님께서, 사장님께서”. The verb is in the “-(으)시-” form (“오셨다, 하신다, 계신다”), and some words change (“계시다, 드시다, 주무시다, 말씀하시다”). It can be followed by “는/도”: “께서는, 께서도”. The honoured person as a receiver takes “께” (a different particle); as subject, “께서”. It is used in speech and writing; in casual speech “이/가” is also common with “-시-”.

examples.en: The teacher wrote on the board.
My grandfather takes a walk every morning.
The president is in a meeting now.
My parents trusted me.
The kimchi that my mother sent has arrived.

compare.difference: “이/가” is neutral; “께서” adds respect. Both go with the honorific verb.
“께서” marks who does it; “께” marks who receives it.

pair.en: I gave it to the teacher.

pitfalls.note: The verb also needs the honorific “-시-”.
“께서” is only for a person to honour.

topik_tip: Honorific subjects bring a set: “께서”, “-시-”, and the special verbs (“계시다, 드시다, 주무시다”).

label: topic or contrast
meaning_en: The topic particle “은/는”: it presents the thing the sentence is about (“as for X”), marks what is already known or generic, and sets a thing against others (contrast). In the curriculum list this row is the contrast use.
usage: After a consonant it is “은”, after a vowel “는”: “책은, 저는”. Topic: “서울은 한국의 수도입니다”. Known information: a thing mentioned before takes “은/는” (“영화를 봤어요. 영화는 재미있었어요”). Contrast: “커피는 마시지만 차는 안 마셔요”. Negatives and “에는/에서는/까지는” often carry it (“주말에는”). Compare the focus of “이/가”. In questions the topic is the item being asked about (“이름은 뭐예요?”).

examples.ko: 저는 커피는 마시지만 차는 안 마셔요.
examples.en: I drink coffee, but I do not drink tea.
Seoul is the capital of Korea.

examples.ko: 어제 영화를 봤어요. 영화는 아주 재미있었어요.
examples.en: I watched a movie yesterday. The movie was very fun.
Korean is hard, but fun.
On weekends I usually rest at home.

compare.difference: “은/는” is the topic or contrast; “이/가” is the focused subject.
“은/는” singles one thing out; “도” adds another to what was already named.

pair.en: As for coffee, I drink it.

pitfalls.note: A question word asking for identity takes “이/가”, not “은/는”.
“나” becomes “내/제” only before “가”; before “는” it stays “나/저”.

topik_tip: The contrast reading (“A, but B”) is shown by the repeated “은/는” in the two halves.

label: also, even, either
meaning_en: A particle meaning “too, also”, “even”, and, with a negative, “not even ... / not any ...”. It adds one more item to something already named.
usage: It attaches to a noun and replaces “이/가/을/를” (“저도 갔어요”), or follows other particles (“에도, 에서도, 한테도, 까지도”). Repeated, “N도 N도” means “both ... and ...”. With a question word and a negative it means “none” (“아무도, 아무것도, 어디에도, 하나도”). With a counter it stresses a small amount: “한 명도 안 왔다”. “도” can also mean “even” (“점심도 못 먹었어요”).

examples.en: I will come along too.
I was so busy today that I could not even eat lunch.

examples.ko: 이 가게는 가격도 싸고 맛도 좋아요.
examples.en: This shop's prices are low, and the food is good too.
There is no one at home.
Jisu is good at English and at Japanese.

compare.difference: “도” adds (“too”); “만” limits (“only”).
“은/는” sets one thing against others; “도” says it is included as well.

pair.en: As for coffee, I drink it.

pitfalls.note: It replaces “이/가/을/를”; it does not stack on them.
“아무도” needs a negative predicate.
pitfalls.en: There is no one at home.

topik_tip: “도” plus a negative verb (“아무도 안/못 ...”) is the “nobody/nothing” frame.

label: object marker
meaning_en: The object particle “을/를”: it marks what the action is done to: “책을 읽다, 커피를 마시다”. It also marks the place passed through or left (“길을 건너다, 학교를 졸업하다”) and verbal nouns before “하다” (“공부를 하다”).
usage: After a consonant it is “을”, after a vowel “를”: “밥을, 커피를”. In speech it is often dropped (“밥 먹었어?”) or contracted (“나를 → 날”, “저를 → 절”). With “좋아하다, 싫어하다, 사랑하다” the object takes “을/를”, while with the adjectives “좋다, 싫다, 필요하다” the thing takes “이/가”. For “되다” and “아니다” the complement takes “이/가”. After motion verbs, “을/를” marks a path or a place left (“길을 건너다”, “집을 나서다”) and sometimes the destination in speech (“학교를 가다”), though “에” is the standard marker for a destination.

examples.en: I drink coffee every morning.
Jisu sang a song.
Be careful when you cross the crosswalk.
I am studying Korean.
I met a friend yesterday.

compare.difference: “을/를” marks the object of an action; “이/가” marks the subject or the thing described by an adjective.
“책을 읽었어요” is a plain statement; “책은 읽었어요” sets the book against other things.

pair.en: As for the book, I read it.

pitfalls.note: The thing wanted or liked as an adjective takes “이/가”; with the verb “좋아하다” it takes “을/를”.
The complement of “되다” takes “이/가”.

topik_tip: “좋아하다” takes “을/를” and “좋다” takes “이/가”: this pair is a classic.

label: with, and (spoken)
meaning_en: A spoken particle for “with” and “and”: “친구랑 영화를 봤어요” (with a friend), “사과랑 배” (apples and pears). It is the casual counterpart of “과/와” and “하고”.
usage: After a consonant it is “이랑”, after a vowel “랑”: “동생이랑, 친구랑, 나랑”. It marks a partner (“나랑 같이 갈래?”), a list (“김밥이랑 라면을 먹었어요”), and a comparison (“이것이랑 같아요”). It is casual speech; in writing or in a formal talk “과/와” or “하고” is used. For listing, the last noun may carry “랑” too (“사과랑 배랑 포도랑”).

examples.en: I watched a movie with a friend yesterday.
I like apples and pears.
I go to school with my younger sibling.
For lunch I ate gimbap and ramen.
Do you want to go with me?

compare.difference: “이랑” and “하고” are close in speech. “하고” is the more neutral of the two and does not change after a vowel or consonant.
“과/와” is the written form. It sounds stiff in casual talk.

pair.en: I went together with a friend.
I went together with a friend.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel it is “랑”, not “이랑”.
It is a spoken form; a formal report uses “과/와”.
pitfalls.en: Today I will present on the economies of Korea and Japan.

topik_tip: The three “with/and” particles: “과/와” (written), “하고” (neutral), “이랑/랑” (casual).

label: direction, means, role
meaning_en: A particle with several related jobs: direction (“학교로 가다”), means or tool (“지하철로 가다, 펜으로 쓰다, 한국어로 말하다”), material (“나무로 만들다”), role or status (“의사로 일하다”), and cause (“병으로 쉬다”).
usage: After a consonant it is “으로”, after a vowel or ㄹ it is “로”: “집으로, 손으로, 학교로, 서울로, 연필로, 지하철로”. Direction: movement toward, not necessarily arriving. Means: a vehicle, tool or language. Material: what something is made from. Role: “으로 일하다, 으로 지내다”. In “으로 정하다/결정하다” it marks the thing chosen.

examples.en: I commute by subway every day.
This cake is made with rice flour.
The class is conducted in Korean.
I am on my way home.
Jisu works as a doctor.

compare.difference: “에” names the goal where one arrives; “(으)로” names the direction one heads in.
“에서” marks where one comes from (or where an action takes place); “로” marks where one goes.

pitfalls.note: A noun ending in ㄹ takes “로”.
After a consonant other than ㄹ it is “으로”.

topik_tip: Pick “으로” or “로” by the last sound of the noun: ㄹ and vowels give “로”, other consonants give “으로”.

label: from (start of time or order)
meaning_en: A particle for a starting point: “from, starting at”, in time (“아홉 시부터”), in order (“밥부터 먹다”), and in a range with “까지”. It also marks what comes first: “먼저 ... 부터”.
usage: It attaches to nouns of time, number or order: “아침부터, 월요일부터, 처음부터, 어디부터”. “N부터 N까지” expresses a range. With the verb “시작하다” it names when something starts. For a place of origin the standard particle is “에서” (“서울에서 왔어요”). In “밥부터 먹자” it means “let's start with eating”, and “부터” can be followed by “는” (“오늘부터는”).

examples.en: Class starts at nine.
From tomorrow I will exercise every day.
I go to school from Monday to Friday.
Let's eat first and then talk.
Where shall we start reading together?

compare.difference: “부터” is a start in time or order; “에서” is a start in place.

pair.en: I have been walking since morning.

compare.difference: “에” puts something at one point in time; “부터” gives the point from which it continues.

pitfalls.note: A place of origin takes “에서”.
It is attached directly, with no “에” in front.

topik_tip: The frame “N부터 N까지” (from ... to ...) is among the first patterns tested.

label: at, to, on (time, place, target)
meaning_en: A particle with several basic jobs: a point in time (“세 시에”), the place where something exists or one is going (“책상 위에, 학교에”), a target of an action on a thing (“꽃에 물을 주다”), a cause (“바람에 쓰러지다”) and a rate (“하루에 세 번”).
usage: It attaches to nouns. Time: clock times, days, months and seasons (“일곱 시에, 월요일에, 겨울에”); the words “오늘, 어제, 내일, 지금, 언제, 그때” do not take “에”. Existence and destination: “집에 있다, 학교에 가다, 서울에 살다”. Target: for a thing or place that receives (“꽃에 물을 주다, 벽에 그림을 걸다”); a person receives “에게/한테”. Rate: “하루에 세 번, 한 개에 천 원”. For a place where an action happens, “에서” is used.

examples.en: I get up at seven in the morning.
I meet a friend on the weekend.
There is a book on the desk.
I am going to school tomorrow.
Take the medicine three times a day.
I watered the flowers.

compare.difference: “에” names where something is or where one goes; “에서” names where an action happens.
“에” marks a thing or place that receives; “에게” marks a person or animal.

pair.en: I gave water to the flowers.
I gave a present to my friend.

pitfalls.note: “어제, 오늘, 내일, 지금” take no “에”.
A verb of existence takes “에”, not “에서”.

topik_tip: “에” (point in time, place of existence, destination) versus “에서” (place of action) is the most tested particle contrast at this level.

label: to (a person or animal)
meaning_en: A particle for the person or animal that receives an action or is its target: “친구에게 선물을 주다, 동생에게 전화하다”. It is the written and neutral form of the spoken “한테”.
usage: It attaches to a person or animal noun: “친구에게, 어머니에게, 강아지에게”. Verbs: “주다, 보내다, 말하다, 묻다, 가르치다, 전화하다, 쓰다”. It also marks the source with “받다, 듣다, 배우다” (“선생님에게 칭찬을 듣다”), and the doer in a passive (“개에게 물리다”). A person to be honoured takes “께”; a thing or place takes “에”. After it, “는/도/만” can follow (“친구에게는”).

examples.en: I gave a present to my friend.
I made a phone call to my mother.
I sent a letter to Jisu.
I read a book to my younger sibling.
I was praised by the teacher.

compare.difference: “에게” and “한테” mean the same. “한테” is spoken; “에게” is neutral and also fits writing.
“에게” is for a person or animal; “에” is for a thing or place.

pair.en: I gave my younger sibling some water.

pitfalls.note: A place takes “에”, not “에게”.
A plant or a thing takes “에”.

topik_tip: The honorific partner is “께”; the spoken partner is “한테”; the source version is “에게서”.

label: at (action), from (origin)
meaning_en: A particle with two main jobs: the place where an action happens (“도서관에서 공부하다”) and the place something comes from or starts (“한국에서 왔다, 부산에서 서울까지”). With a group as the subject it works like “이/가” (“회사에서 발표했다”).
usage: It attaches to place nouns: “집에서, 학교에서, 서울에서”. Action: “공부하다, 만나다, 일하다, 먹다”. Origin and range: “오다, 출발하다, 나오다” and “N에서 N까지”. A group or institution as subject: “정부에서, 학교에서, 회사에서”. For a place of existence the particle is “에” (“집에 있다”); for a person as the source it is “에게서/한테서”. “서울에 살다” and “서울에서 살다” are both used with “살다”.

examples.en: I study in the library.
We met at school.
I went from Busan to Seoul by train.
I came from Vietnam.
The company announced a new product.

compare.difference: “에서” is where an action happens; “에” is where something is or where one goes.
“에서” marks a place as the source; “에게서” marks a person.

pair.en: A letter came from a friend.

pitfalls.note: The place of an action takes “에서”.
A person as the source takes “에게서”, not “에서”.
pitfalls.en: I received a present from a friend.

topik_tip: Remember the pair “에 있다” (be at) and “에서 -하다” (do at).

label: possessive “of, 's”
meaning_en: A particle linking two nouns: possession (“친구의 가방”), part of (“책의 제목”), relation or origin (“한국의 수도, 어머니의 사랑”). It is pronounced like “에” in speech, and often left out.
usage: It attaches to the first noun: “N의 N”. With pronouns it contracts: “나의 → 내, 저의 → 제, 너의 → 네” (“제 가방, 내 친구”); “우리의” becomes “우리” without it. In compounds a noun used as a classifier takes no “의” (“한국 음식, 학교 친구”). The particle is written “의” though in ordinary speech it is pronounced like “에”. It is not attached to verbs or adjectives; those use modifier endings.

examples.en: This is my friend's bag.
Seoul is the capital of Korea.
Today's weather in Seoul is clear.
A parent's love has no end.
My hobby is taking photos.

compare.difference: “저의” and “제” are the same; “제” is the contracted form that is usual in speech.
A noun that describes the type needs no “의”. “의” expresses belonging or relation.

pair.en: We introduce the food of Korea.

pitfalls.note: The particle is spelled “의”, even though it is pronounced like “에”.
“내, 제, 네” already contain the possessive: do not add “의”.

topik_tip: Possessive pronouns contract (“제, 내, 네”) and then take no “의”.

label: and; with (neutral spoken)
meaning_en: A particle that joins nouns (“A and B”) and marks a partner or a standard of comparison (“with”). It is the neutral spoken form, between the casual “이랑” and the written “과/와”.
usage: It attaches to any noun, with no change after a vowel or a consonant: “사과하고 배, 친구하고 같이, 이것하고 저것”. Listing: “N하고 N”. Partner: “친구하고 만나다, 선생님하고 이야기하다”. Comparison: “N하고 같다/다르다”. The speaker can also place it after the last noun (“사과하고 배하고”). It does not mark the receiver of a gift or message: that is “에게/한테”.

examples.en: I like apples and pears.
I had lunch together with a friend.
This and that are very different.
Today I went to the market with Mom.
I decided after talking with the teacher.

compare.difference: “하고” and “이랑” are near-synonyms in speech; “이랑” is more casual.
“과/와” is the written form and sounds stiff in casual speech.

pair.en: I bought a book and a notebook.
I bought a book and a notebook.

pitfalls.note: It means “with” or “and”, not “to”: the receiver of a gift takes “에게/한테”.
pitfalls.en: I gave my friend a present.

topik_tip: Do not confuse the particle “하고” with the verb “하다” + “-고”: it joins nouns.

label: only, just that one
meaning_en: A particle meaning “only, just”: it limits something to one thing and excludes the rest. It can also stress a minimum (“한 번만”).
usage: It attaches to a noun, a counter phrase, an adverb or another particle: “커피만, 두 명만, 집에서만, 너에게만”. It replaces “이/가/을/를” (“저만 갔어요”, “커피만 마셔요”) and sits after others (“에서만, 에게만”). It goes with positive and negative predicates alike. For “only + a negative verb” the particle “밖에” is used; for “only” at the end of a sentence “뿐이다”. “이번만” means “just this once”.

examples.en: I only drink coffee.
Only two students were in the classroom.
Today I rested only at home.

examples.ko: 이 일은 지수만 할 수 있어요.
examples.en: Only Jisu can do this job.
Please help me, just this once.

compare.difference: “만” limits (“only”); “도” adds (“too”).
“만” goes with a positive or negative verb. “밖에” needs a negative and suggests the amount is small.

pitfalls.note: “만” replaces “을/를”; it does not stand next to it.

topik_tip: “만” (any predicate), “밖에” (negative predicate) and “뿐” (with “이다”) are three ways to say only.

label: to be: “X is Y” copula
meaning_en: The copula “to be”: it joins two nouns (“A is B”), names what something is, and in the negative is replaced by the adjective “아니다”. It is the one word that attaches to a noun and works like a verb or adjective, so it takes every ending and politeness level.
usage: It is written attached to the noun, with no space (“학생이다”, “친구예요”). Plain: “이다” (written, essay and news style); polite: “이에요” after a final consonant and “예요” after a vowel (“학생이에요, 친구예요”); formal: “입니다” (“학생입니다, 친구입니다”). After a vowel the “이” may drop in speech and informal writing (“친구다”, “친구고”, “친구라서”), but never after a consonant (“학생이다, 학생이고, 학생이라서”). Past: “이었다/였다” (“학생이었어요, 친구였어요”). The negative is “N이/가 아니다” (“학생이 아니에요”), never “안 이다”. The syllable “이” here is not the subject particle “이/가”, though the two look alike.

examples.en: I am a Korean university student.
This is my friend.
Seoul is the capital of Korea.

examples.ko: 이 제품은 올해 가장 많이 팔린 노트북입니다.
examples.en: This product is the best-selling laptop of the year.
That place used to be a small bookshop.
The biggest problem is time.

compare.difference: “이다” states that A is B; “아니다” denies it. The noun takes the particle “이/가” before “아니다”, but “이다” attaches to the noun directly. Both inflect like ordinary predicates, so “학생이 아니에요” is a complete polite sentence.

The subject particle “이/가” marks who or what does or is something and comes before another word; the copula “이다” is itself the predicate and ends the sentence. “선생님이” is a subject, “선생님이에요” is a statement.

pitfalls.note: Negate with “아니다”, not with “안” before “이다”.
“예요” belongs only after a vowel. After a final consonant use “이에요”.
“이다” is attached to the noun; do not leave a space before it.

topik_tip: Tell the copula from the subject particle by what follows: “책이다, 책이에요, 책이고” end or continue a predicate, while “책이 있다” has a verb after it. In 쓰기, the plain “-이다” (“서울은 수도이다”) is the written-register form; do not mix it with “-이에요” in one text.

label: to (a person), spoken
meaning_en: The spoken form of “에게”: it marks the person or animal that receives an action: “친구한테 전화하다”. It also marks the source with “받다/듣다” and the doer in a passive (“선생님한테 혼나다”).
usage: It attaches to a person or animal: “친구한테, 엄마한테, 강아지한테”. Verbs: “주다, 말하다, 묻다, 보내다, 전화하다, 가르치다”; “받다, 듣다, 배우다” for a source (“친구한테 선물을 받았어요”); a passive doer (“혼나다, 잡히다, 물리다”). A source can also take “한테서”. It is colloquial; in writing “에게” is used. A thing or a place takes “에”, and an honoured person “께”.

examples.en: I called Mom yesterday.
I received a present from a friend.
I fed the puppy.
I got scolded by the teacher yesterday.
Who did you hear that story from?

compare.difference: The two have the same meaning; “에게” is neutral and also used in writing.
“께” replaces “한테/에게” for a person to be honoured.

pair.en: I gave it to my younger sibling.
I gave it to my grandmother.

pitfalls.note: A plant or a thing takes “에”.

topik_tip: In listening items “한테” and “에게” are interchangeable; “께” signals an honoured person.

label: than (comparison)
meaning_en: A particle for the standard of a comparison: “A는 B보다 ...” means “A is more ... than B”. It is often combined with “더” (“more”) or “훨씬” (“much”).
usage: It attaches to the thing that is compared against: “부산보다, 어제보다, 생각보다, 저보다”. The predicate is a comparable adjective or adverb: “크다, 많다, 빠르다, 좋아하다”. Frames: “A가 B보다 더 ...”, “B보다 A를 더 좋아하다”. “생각보다” (than I thought) and “기대보다” (than expected) are frequent set phrases. Equal comparisons use “만큼” or “처럼”. “보다” can also be an adverb meaning “more” (“보다 좋은 방법”).

examples.en: Seoul has a larger population than Busan.
Today is colder than yesterday.
I like tea more than coffee.
This bag is much lighter than I thought.
My younger sibling is taller than I am.

compare.difference: “보다” says one is more; “만큼” says they are equal.

pair.en: They run as fast as Jisu.

compare.difference: As a bare adverb, “보다” means “more” and compares nothing.

pitfalls.note: It is a particle, so it is attached to the noun without a space.

topik_tip: The set phrase “생각보다” (more ... than I thought) is the most frequent form.

label: will; must be; polite softener
meaning_en: A pre-final ending with three jobs: the speaker's will (“제가 하겠습니다”), a guess about the present or the future (“비가 오겠어요, 힘들겠어요”), and a polite softening in set phrases (“처음 뵙겠습니다, 알겠습니다, 모르겠습니다”).
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems and sits before the final ending: “하다 → 하겠다”, “맛있다 → 맛있겠다”. With the speaker as subject it is a decision made now (“제가 가겠습니다”). With others it is a guess (“그 사람은 지금 바쁘겠어요”). It does not point to the past: a past guess is “-었겠-” (“어제 힘들었겠어요”). Questions “-겠어요?” ask about the listener's will or about a guess. It is typical in “합쇼체” (“-겠습니다”).

examples.en: I will do the dishes today.
Looking at the sky, it will rain soon.
The exam is tomorrow, so you must be very nervous.
Nice to meet you. I look forward to your help.
I do not quite know. Please explain it again.
This food looks really delicious.

compare.difference: “-겠-” voices a decision at the moment of speaking; “-을 거예요” states a plan or a prediction.

pair.en: I am going to do it.

compare.difference: “-겠습니다” is the formal declaration; “-을게요” is the everyday promise.

pitfalls.note: “-겠-” does not mark the past: use “-었겠-” for a guess about the past.
pitfalls.en: It must have been very hard yesterday.

topik_tip: “알겠습니다 / 모르겠습니다 / 처음 뵙겠습니다” are polite formulas, not predictions.

label: past tense
meaning_en: The past tense ending: “-았-/-었-/-였-” before the final ending marks an event or state in the past (“갔다, 먹었다, 했다”). With some verbs and adjectives it also marks a state that holds now as a result of a completed change.
usage: It follows the stem with vowel harmony: “-았-” after ㅏ/ㅗ (“가다 → 갔다, 오다 → 왔다, 살다 → 살았다”), “-었-” after other vowels (“먹다 → 먹었다, 마시다 → 마셨다, 있다 → 있었다”), and “하다 → 했다”. Irregulars: “듣다 → 들었다” (ㄷ), “춥다 → 추웠다” (ㅂ), “쓰다 → 썼다” (ㅡ), “모르다 → 몰랐다” (“르”), “이다 → 이었다/였다”. Some verbs describe a present state in the past form: “결혼했어요” (I am married), “알겠어요”, “닫혔어요”. For an earlier past cut off from now see “-었었-”.

examples.en: I ate bibimbap for lunch yesterday.
It rained yesterday, so I stayed at home.
I came to Korea last year.
I was short when I was little.
No, I am already married.
The subway was very crowded this morning.

compare.difference: “-었-” reports a past event; “-었었-” adds that it is over and cut off from the present.

pair.en: I lived in Seoul last year.
I used to live in Seoul last year.

compare.difference: “-었-” looks back, “-겠-” looks ahead or makes a guess.

pitfalls.note: A ㄷ-irregular verb turns ㄷ into ㄹ before a vowel.
A ㅂ-irregular adjective becomes “웠”.

topik_tip: “결혼했어요” (I am married) and “알았어요” (I understand) use the past form for a present state.

label: honorific subject marker
meaning_en: The honorific infix that shows respect for the subject of the sentence: “선생님이 오셨다”. It goes between the stem and the ending and is always about the person who does or has the action, never the listener unless they are the subject.
usage: After a vowel it is “-시-”, after a consonant “-으시-”: “가다 → 가시다, 읽다 → 읽으시다”; a ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ (“살다 → 사시다, 만들다 → 만드시다, 알다 → 아시다”). It combines with “-었-” as “-(으)셨-” and with endings (“-세요, -십니다”). Some verbs have honorific words: “먹다 → 드시다, 자다 → 주무시다, 있다 → 계시다, 말하다 → 말씀하시다”. “있으시다” is used for having (“시간이 있으세요?”). Do not use it for things: “커피 나오셨습니다” is an over-honorific.

examples.en: When the teacher came into the classroom, the students stood up.

examples.ko: 할머니는 매일 아침 일찍 일어나시고 산책을 하세요.
examples.en: My grandmother gets up early every morning and takes a walk.
The president is in a meeting now.

examples.ko: 어머니는 요리를 잘하시고 노래도 잘 부르세요.
examples.en: My mother cooks well and also sings well.
Please eat plenty, and enjoy it.

compare.difference: The subject particle “께서” and the infix “-으시-” usually go together.
Some verbs have a separate honorific word: “드시다” replaces “먹으시다”.

pair.en: My younger sibling eats a meal.

pitfalls.note: Use the honorific verb: “드시다”, not “먹으시다”.
A thing is not honoured.
A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-시-”.

topik_tip: The three honorific tools are the subject particle “께서”, the infix “-(으)시-” and special words like “드시다/계시다”.

label: and, then (listing, sequence)
meaning_en: A connective ending that lists equal facts (“키가 크고 잘생겼다”) or links actions in order (“밥을 먹고 학교에 갔다”). It says nothing about cause: the two parts are just joined.
usage: It attaches to any stem without a change: “크다 → 크고”, “먹다 → 먹고”, “학생이다 → 학생이고”. Tense is shown once, on the final verb (“-었다”), and it applies to the whole sentence: “어제 영화를 보고 저녁을 먹었어요”. A tense inside the first clause (“-었고”) is possible for a finished state. The subject may be the same or different. For simultaneous actions “-으면서” is used; “-고 있다” is a different pattern (progressive).

examples.en: Jisu is tall and also sings well.

examples.ko: 저는 아침에 운동을 하고 샤워를 해요.
examples.en: In the morning I exercise and then take a shower.
Seoul has many people and the traffic is complicated.
Yesterday I watched a movie and had dinner.

examples.ko: 이 가게는 싸고 맛있어서 인기가 많아요.
examples.en: This shop is cheap and tasty, so it is popular.

compare.difference: “-고” joins actions in order or lists facts; “-으면서” says that they happen at the same time.
“-어서” makes the first action a step toward the second or its cause. “-고” just links them.

pair.en: I washed it and ate it.

pitfalls.note: The tense goes on the last verb and covers the whole sentence.
pitfalls.en: Yesterday I watched a movie and had dinner.

topik_tip: “-고” is the all-purpose “and”: it is a safe first choice, and “-고 나서” adds emphasis on completion.

label: because, since; when I did X, I found
meaning_en: A connective ending for a reason that the speaker stresses, and it can be followed by a command or a suggestion. It also introduces something the speaker finds after doing something (“열어 보니까 비어 있었다”).
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-니까”, after other consonants “-으니까”: “가다 → 가니까, 먹다 → 먹으니까, 살다 → 사니까 (ㄹ drops), 춥다 → 추우니까, 듣다 → 들으니까, 학생이다 → 학생이니까”; the past is “-었으니까”. The main clause may be a command, a request or a suggestion: “비가 오니까 우산을 가져가세요”, “바쁘니까 나중에 하자”. In the discovery use the main clause is a past observation. Sentence-final “-으니까요” gives a reason in speech.

examples.en: It is raining, so take an umbrella.
I am busy now, so I will call later.
The weather is nice, so shall we go for a walk?
When I went home, nobody was there.
I am fine, so please eat first.

compare.difference: “-으니까” can be followed by a command or suggestion; “-어서” cannot.

pair.en: It is raining, so take an umbrella.
It rained, so I bought an umbrella.

compare.difference: “-으니” is the shorter, more written form of “-으니까” with the same range of main clauses.

pair.en: It is cold, so put on clothes.
It is cold, so put on clothes.

pitfalls.note: A command or a suggestion follows “-으니까”, not “-어서”.
pitfalls.en: It is raining, so take an umbrella.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “니”.
pitfalls.en: Since I live in this neighborhood, it is convenient.

topik_tip: A reason followed by a command or “-ㅂ시다/-자” takes “-으니까”; a plain cause takes “-어서”.

label: in order to (go or come)
meaning_en: A connective ending for the purpose of going or coming somewhere: “to do X”. It is followed by a verb of motion such as “가다, 오다, 다니다, 나가다, 들어오다”.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-러”, after other consonants “-으러”: “사다 → 사러”, “놀다 → 놀러” (the ㄹ stays), “먹다 → 먹으러”, “듣다 → 들으러” (ㄷ becomes ㄹ), “걷다 → 걸으러”. The main verb must show movement: “밥을 먹으러 식당에 가요”. It cannot be followed by other verbs (“공부하러 일찍 일어났어요” is wrong). The common invitation is “놀러 오세요”. It takes no tense.

examples.en: I am going to a restaurant to eat lunch.
I went to Seoul to meet a friend.
I came to the library to borrow a book.
Please come over to my house some time.
I came to Korea to learn Korean.

compare.difference: “-으러” needs a motion verb after it. “-으려고” takes any verb.

pair.en: I got up early to drink coffee.

compare.difference: “-기 위해(서)” is the formal way and goes with any main verb.

pair.en: I went to the library to study.
I went to the library in order to study.

pitfalls.note: The main verb must be a motion verb; otherwise use “-으려고”.
pitfalls.en: I got up early to study.

pitfalls.note: A ㄷ-irregular verb turns ㄷ into ㄹ.
pitfalls.en: I am going to listen to music.

topik_tip: The frame is “N을/를 V-러 가다/오다”: a purpose plus a motion verb.

label: so, and then (cause, sequence)
meaning_en: A connective ending for a cause or reason (“비가 와서 못 갔어요”), for an action followed by another that depends on it (“서울에 가서 친구를 만났어요”), and for means (“걸어서 가다”).
usage: It attaches to stems with “-아/어”: “오다 → 와서”, “먹다 → 먹어서”, “하다 → 해서”, “예쁘다 → 예뻐서”, “춥다 → 추워서”, “듣다 → 들어서”, “모르다 → 몰라서”, “학생이다 → 학생이어서”. It takes no tense of its own (“늦었어서” is wrong) and the main clause cannot be a command or a suggestion. For sequence it is typical with “가다, 오다, 앉다, 일어나다, 만들다” (“앉아서 이야기하다”). Fixed phrases: “늦어서 죄송합니다, 감사해서”.

examples.en: It rained a lot, so I stayed at home.
I am sorry for being very late.
I went to Seoul and met a friend there.
I walk to school every morning.
I am a student, so I have a lot of time.
The road was jammed, so I was late for the appointment.

compare.difference: “-으니까” may be followed by a command or suggestion; “-어서” may not.

pair.en: I was tired, so I rested.

compare.difference: “-어서” links an action to the next one that follows from it; “-고” only lists them in order.

pair.en: I washed it and ate it.

pitfalls.note: The tense goes on the last verb, not on “-어서”.
pitfalls.en: I am sorry for being late.

pitfalls.note: A command or suggestion does not follow “-어서”.

topik_tip: “-어서” for cause and sequence, “-으니까” when a command follows: a standard choice question.

label: but, although
meaning_en: A connective ending for contrast: “X, but Y”. It admits the first statement and adds something that does not follow from it. It is also a polite opener before a request: “죄송하지만, 실례지만”.
usage: It attaches to any stem without a change (verbs, adjectives, “이다”), with tense if needed: “어렵다 → 어렵지만”, “좋아하다 → 좋아하지만”, “갔다 → 갔지만”, “학생이다 → 학생이지만”. The stem keeps its form: “춥다 → 춥지만”, “살다 → 살지만”. The two clauses must contrast. “죄송하지만 창문 좀 닫아 주세요” (sorry to trouble you, but...) is a frequent frame. A softer link is “-는데”, and a formal written one is “-으나”.

examples.en: Korean is hard, but fun.

examples.ko: 저는 커피를 좋아하지만 하루에 한 잔만 마셔요.
examples.en: I like coffee, but I drink only one cup a day.
Sorry to trouble you, but please close the window.
It rained, but we went on the picnic.
This outfit is pretty, but it is too expensive.

compare.difference: “-지만” is a firm “but”. “-는데” is looser: it can only set the scene.

pair.en: This outfit is pretty, but expensive.
This outfit is pretty, but expensive.

compare.difference: “-지만” grants a fact (“it is raining, but”); “-어도” grants a supposition (“even if”).

pair.en: It is raining, but I will go.
I will go even if it rains.

pitfalls.note: The two clauses must contrast; a plain reason does not fit.
pitfalls.en: I was hungry, so I ate.

topik_tip: A contrast frame like “어렵지만 재미있다” is the pattern most often seen; check that the two halves oppose each other.

label: in order to, intending to
meaning_en: A connective ending for the purpose or intention of the speaker: “in order to X, intending to X”. The main clause is what is done for that purpose (“한국어를 배우려고 한국에 왔어요”). With “하다” it means “intend to”: “-으려고 하다”.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-려고”, after other consonants “-으려고”: “배우다 → 배우려고”, “먹다 → 먹으려고”, “살다 → 살려고” (ㄹ stays), “만들다 → 만들려고”, “듣다 → 들으려고” (ㄷ becomes ㄹ), “눕다 → 누우려고”. It attaches to verbs only, takes no tense, and the subject of both clauses is the same. The main clause is a statement or a question about what is done. The pattern for “to go/come in order to” is “-으러”.

examples.en: I came to Korea to learn Korean.

examples.ko: 친구에게 줄 선물을 사려고 백화점에 갔어요.
examples.en: I went to the department store to buy a present for a friend.
I set an alarm in order to get up early.
I exercise every day to lose weight.
I took a taxi so as not to be late.

compare.difference: “-으러” goes only with “가다/오다”; “-으려고” goes with any verb.

pair.en: I went to the library to study.
I got up early to study.

compare.difference: “-으려고” gives the purpose of an action; “-으려면” sets the purpose as a condition for what is needed.

pair.en: I study in order to pass.
To pass, you have to study.

pitfalls.note: The first verb takes no tense ending.
pitfalls.en: I came to Korea to learn Korean.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ before “-려고”.
pitfalls.en: I take care of my health in order to live long.

topik_tip: The purpose frame with the same subject is “-으려고”; different subjects need “-게/-도록”.

label: formal polite question
meaning_en: The question ending of the formal polite speech level (“합쇼체”): “-ㅂ니까?” after a vowel and “-습니까?” after a consonant. It is used in business, news, service and speeches to ask politely.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-ㅂ니까”, after a consonant “-습니까”: “가다 → 갑니까”, “먹다 → 먹습니까”, “살다 → 삽니까” and “만들다 → 만듭니까” (the ㄹ drops), “이다 → 입니까”. It goes with the honorific (“가십니까, 하셨습니까”), the past (“-었습니까”) and “-겠습니까”. The answer is “-ㅂ니다/-습니다”. Everyday politeness in speech uses “-어요?”. It is not used for questions to children or equals in casual talk.

examples.en: Where are you going now?
Have you had your lunch?
What is your name, sir?
Where did you work yesterday?
Have you read this book?

compare.difference: “-습니까” is formal. “-어요?” is the everyday polite question.
Both are polite; “-으세요?” is the gentler everyday honorific question, “-으십니까?” is the formal one.

pitfalls.note: A vowel stem takes “-ㅂ니까”, not “-습니까”.
A ㄹ-stem drops its ㄹ.

topik_tip: The formal question “-ㅂ니까/-습니까” is answered with “-ㅂ니다/-습니다”.

label: formal polite statement
meaning_en: The statement ending of the formal polite speech level (“합쇼체”): “-ㅂ니다” after a vowel and “-습니다” after a consonant. It is used in speeches, news, announcements, presentations and with customers.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-ㅂ니다”, after a consonant “-습니다”: “가다 → 갑니다”, “먹다 → 먹습니다”, “살다 → 삽니다” and “만들다 → 만듭니다” (the ㄹ drops), “이다 → 입니다”. Past “-었습니다”, future and softening “-겠습니다”, honorific “-(으)십니다”. It is more formal than “-어요”, which is the everyday polite level. The question is “-ㅂ니까?/-습니까?”. Typical set expressions: “감사합니다, 죄송합니다, 알겠습니다”.

examples.en: I study Korean.
I live in Seoul.
Today's meeting starts at three.
This product is of very high quality.
Thank you for helping so much.

compare.difference: “-습니다” is the formal level for speeches and service. “-어요” is the soft everyday polite level.
“-습니다” speaks to a listener formally. “-는다” (“한다체”) is the plain written style with no listener.

pitfalls.note: A vowel stem takes “-ㅂ니다”.
A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ.

topik_tip: In listening and reading, the “합쇼체” (“-ㅂ니다”) marks formal, public speech.

label: formal let's
meaning_en: A formal suggestion ending: “let's do X”. It is addressed to equals or juniors in formal or group settings: meetings, notices, slogans, teachers to a class. The polite “-어요” or “-을까요?” is used instead for people to be respected.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-ㅂ시다”, after other consonants “-읍시다”: “하다 → 합시다”, “가다 → 갑시다”, “먹다 → 먹읍시다”, “읽다 → 읽읍시다”, “살다 → 삽시다” and “만들다 → 만듭시다” (the ㄹ drops), “눕다 → 누웁시다” (ㅂ-irregular), “듣다 → 들읍시다” (ㄷ-irregular), “모으다 → 모읍시다”. The negative is “-지 맙시다”. It is used for a joint action that includes the speaker, with a firm tone that is not suitable when addressing someone senior.

examples.en: Let's leave work early today.
Let's have lunch together.
Let's all pool our strength.
Let's live helping each other.
Let's not make noise during class.

compare.difference: “-자” is the plain, casual “let's” for close friends and juniors. “-ㅂ시다” is formal and public.
“-ㅂ시다” proposes firmly; “-을까요?” asks whether the other agrees.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-ㅂ시다”.
A ㅂ-irregular verb turns ㅂ into “우”.
pitfalls.en: Let's lie down for a moment.

topik_tip: The exam often tests the choice between “-ㅂ시다” (vowel stem) and “-읍시다” (consonant stem).

label: polite honorific ending
meaning_en: The honorific form of the polite “해요체”: “-(으)세요” means “you/they do (honoured)”, or “please do ...”. By context it states, asks or requests: “어디 가세요?” (Where are you going?), “앉으세요” (Please sit).
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-세요”, after other consonants “-으세요”: “가다 → 가세요”, “읽다 → 읽으세요”, “앉다 → 앉으세요”, “살다 → 사세요” and “만들다 → 만드세요” (the ㄹ drops), “듣다 → 들으세요”. Special verbs: “먹다 → 드세요, 자다 → 주무세요, 있다 → 계세요, 말하다 → 말씀하세요”. The negative request is “-지 마세요”. It is the common polite request and is gentler than the formal “-으십시오”.

examples.en: Welcome to our shop.
Please sit in this seat.
Where are you going, Teacher?
My mother is cooking in the kitchen now.
Please read this book.

compare.difference: “-으세요” is the everyday polite request; “-으십시오” is formal and typical of notices.
“-어요” is polite but neutral; “-으세요” adds respect for the person doing the action.

pitfalls.note: For a person to honour, “먹다” becomes “드시다”.
A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ.

topik_tip: Meaning depends on the context and intonation: statement, question or request.

label: formal honorific command
meaning_en: The formal honorific command of the “합쇼체”: “please do X”. It is used in notices, announcements, signs, speeches and service talk to a person or a group to be respected.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-십시오”, after other consonants “-으십시오”: “가다 → 가십시오”, “앉다 → 앉으십시오”, “읽다 → 읽으십시오”, “떠나다 → 떠나십시오”, “만들다 → 만드십시오” (the ㄹ drops). Special verbs: “먹다 → 드십시오, 자다 → 주무십시오”. The negative is “-지 마십시오”. It is stiffer than “-으세요” and does not suit casual talk. The request with “주다” is “-어 주십시오”. “안녕히 가십시오” (goodbye to someone leaving) is a set phrase.

examples.en: Passengers, please take your seats.
Please leave this place right now.
Please read this passage to the end.
Well then, goodbye.
After use, be sure to wash your hands.

compare.difference: “-으십시오” is the formal order of notices; “-으세요” is the milder everyday request.
“-어 주십시오” asks for a favour; the bare “-으십시오” is an order or an instruction.

pair.en: Please close the door for me.

pitfalls.note: A vowel stem takes “-십시오”.
Use “드시다” for eating: “드십시오”.

topik_tip: Notices on signs often end in “-(으)십시오”; the negative is “-지 마십시오”.

label: trailing “and ...” in speech
meaning_en: A sentence-final “-고” in casual speech: the speaker adds a fact and leaves the sentence open, as if more follows (“and ...”). It often answers a question by listing: “친구 만났고, 영화도 봤고.”.
usage: It attaches to any stem, with tense if needed (“만났고, 좋고, 선생님이고”), and the sentence stops there. The tone is casual (“해체”), and with a polite listener it is “-고요”: “저는 한국어 선생님이고요.”. It adds to what was said before: a list, an afterthought, or a second reason. It is a spoken version of the connective “-고”. It does not stand as the first and only remark.

examples.en: Yesterday I met a friend, and watched a movie, too.
The exam is over, too. Now I should rest a bit.
I am a Korean teacher. And my hobby is cooking.
The weather is nice. And my mood is good, too.
The place is close, too. And the rent is cheap.

compare.difference: In the middle of a sentence “-고” links two clauses. At the end it adds a fact and leaves the sentence open.

pair.en: It rains and the wind blows.
It is raining. And the wind is blowing too.

compare.difference: “-고” adds another fact; “-거든” gives a reason that explains.

pair.en: It is cold. And it is snowing too.
It is cold. It is snowing, you see.

pitfalls.note: To a person you speak politely to, add “요”.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, I am a student, and so on.

topik_tip: The ending “-고요” is the polite version and appears in interview answers as a way to add information.

label: shall we? I wonder
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending with three jobs: a suggestion (“같이 갈까요?” shall we go together?), an offer (“제가 도와 드릴까요?” shall I help?), and a wondering (“비가 올까?” I wonder if it will rain).
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-ㄹ까”, after other consonants “-을까”: “가다 → 갈까”, “먹다 → 먹을까”, “놀다 → 놀까” and “만들다 → 만들까” (the ㄹ stays), “듣다 → 들을까”, “눕다 → 누울까”. The polite form is “-ㄹ까요?”. With the subject “we” it suggests; with “I” it offers or asks for the listener's will; with others it wonders. A suggestion “-ㅂ시다” is more firm, and a question about the listener's own wish is “-을래?”.

examples.en: Shall we have lunch together?
Shall I open the door for you?
Will it rain tomorrow?
I wonder if this outfit will suit me.
What shall we eat in the evening?

compare.difference: “-을까요?” asks whether the other agrees; “-ㅂ시다” proposes firmly.
“-을까?” proposes something for both; “-을래?” asks what the listener wants to do.

pair.en: Do you want to go together?

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ: “놀다” gives “놀까요”.

topik_tip: The same ending can suggest, offer or wonder: check the subject (we, I, someone else).

label: casual or polite ending
meaning_en: The basic spoken ending: “-어” is the casual “해체” and “-어요” is the polite “해요체”. It is used for statements, questions, requests and suggestions, and the meaning depends on the context and the intonation.
usage: It attaches to the stem with vowel harmony: “가다 → 가(요)”, “오다 → 와(요)”, “보다 → 봐(요)”, “먹다 → 먹어(요)”, “마시다 → 마셔(요)”, “주다 → 줘(요)”, “하다 → 해(요)”, “쓰다 → 써(요)”, “춥다 → 추워(요)”, “듣다 → 들어(요)”, “모르다 → 몰라(요)”. After a noun the copula is “이야/야” and “이에요/예요”. A rising tone makes a question and a falling tone a statement. The honorific is “-세요”; a formal level is “-ㅂ니다”.

examples.en: What are you doing now? Are you busy?
I drink coffee every morning.
This outfit is pretty. Where did you buy it?
It is raining. Take an umbrella.
The food at this restaurant is really delicious.

compare.difference: “-어요” is everyday polite; “-습니다” is formal.
“-어요” is neutral; “-으세요” honours the subject.

pitfalls.note: “하다” becomes “해”, never “하어”.
A ㅂ-irregular adjective turns ㅂ into “우”.

topik_tip: Without “요” it is casual (“해체”); with “요” it is polite (“해요체”).

label: is not (a noun)
meaning_en: The negation of “이다”: “N이/가 아니다” means “is not N”. It denies an identification, not an action (for that, “안” or “-지 않다”).
usage: After a consonant it is “이 아니다”, after a vowel “가 아니다”: “학생이 아니에요”, “의사가 아니에요”. The noun before it takes “이/가” (not “은/는” or “을/를”) as complement: “저는 학생이 아니에요”. Endings: “아니에요, 아닙니다, 아니야, 아니었어요, 아니고”. “N이/가 아니라 M이다” means “not N but M”. The word “아니요” (no) is a separate reply word.

examples.en: I am not a student. I am an office worker.
This is not my bag.
That person is not a doctor but a nurse.
Today is not Monday. It is Tuesday.

examples.ko: 이 길은 우리 집으로 가는 길이 아니었다.
examples.en: This road was not the way to our house.

compare.difference: “이/가 아니다” denies what something is; “-지 않다” denies an action or a quality.

pair.en: I do not go to school.

compare.difference: “아니요” is a reply meaning “no”; “아니다” is the verb of the sentence.

pair.en: No, I am not a student.

pitfalls.note: The noun before “아니다” takes “이/가”, not “을/를”.
The verb is “아니다”, not “안이다”.

topik_tip: “N이/가 아니라 N이다” (not N but N) is a frequent frame.

label: want to
meaning_en: An expression for the speaker's own wish: “want to X”. It is used in statements about oneself and in questions to the listener. For another person's wish, “-고 싶어 하다” is used.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with no change: “가다 → 가고 싶다”, “먹다 → 먹고 싶다”, “되다 → 되고 싶다”. The past is “-고 싶었다”, the negative “-고 싶지 않다”. The object may take “을/를” or “이/가” (“커피를/커피가 마시고 싶어요”). It does not attach to adjectives: “예뻐지다” first (“예뻐지고 싶어요”). In speech “-고 싶은데” is often an opening (“커피 마시고 싶은데 같이 갈래요?”). For a third person in a plain statement it is “-고 싶어 하다”.

examples.en: I want to go to Korea.
I do not want to do anything today.
What do you want to eat?
When I was little, I wanted to become a singer.
I feel like having coffee; do you want to come along?

compare.difference: “-고 싶다” is the speaker's own wish; “-고 싶어 하다” reports someone else's.
“-고 싶다” is wanting to do something; “-으면 좋겠다” hopes for a situation.

pair.en: I want to leave work early.
I wish I could leave work early.

pitfalls.note: An adjective does not take “-고 싶다”; use “-어지다” first.
For a third person in a statement, “싶어 하다” is used.

topik_tip: First person and questions to the listener take “-고 싶다”; third person takes “-고 싶어 하다”.

label: be doing (progressive)
meaning_en: An expression for an action in progress: “be -ing”. It also marks a continuing state with a few verbs: wearing (“입고 있다, 쓰고 있다, 들고 있다”), knowing and living (“알고 있다, 살고 있다”), and a habit over a period (“요즘 -고 있다”).
usage: It attaches to verb stems with no change: “먹다 → 먹고 있다”, “기다리다 → 기다리고 있다”, “살다 → 살고 있다”. The tense is on “있다”: “-고 있었다” (was doing). The honorific is “-고 계시다”. With dressing verbs it is ambiguous between the act of putting on (“입고 있다” could mean the process) and the state of wearing. For a state that results from a change of the subject itself (“앉다, 열리다”), the pattern is “-어 있다”. It is not attached to adjectives.

examples.en: What are you doing now?
I am waiting for a friend.
Jisu is wearing a blue hat.
I am studying Korean these days.
I live in Seoul.

compare.difference: “-고 있다” is an action in progress; “-어 있다” is the state after a change.

pair.en: The child is sitting down onto the chair.
The child is seated on the chair.

compare.difference: “-고 있다” is the general progressive; “-는 중이다” is the precise “in the middle of”.

pair.en: I am studying Korean these days.
I am in the middle of studying Korean now.

pitfalls.note: The tense goes on “있다”, not on the first verb.
An adjective does not take “-고 있다”.

topik_tip: “살고 있다, 알고 있다, 가지고 있다” are states: translate as simple present.

label: have to, must
meaning_en: An expression for necessity: “have to X, must X”. The spoken form is “-어야 돼요”; the equivalent written form is “-어야 하다/합니다”. It states an obligation or a requirement.
usage: It attaches to verb, adjective and “이다” stems with “-아/어”: “가다 → 가야 되다”, “먹다 → 먹어야 되다”, “하다 → 해야 되다”, “듣다 → 들어야 되다”, “쉽다 → 쉬워야 되다”. “되다” takes the tense (“-어야 됐다”) and contracts to “돼” in speech (“돼요”, “되어요” is the same). The negative need is “-지 않아도 되다” (don't have to); the prohibition is “-으면 안 되다”. A frequent partner is “-어야 하다”, which is more formal.

examples.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.

examples.ko: 숙제를 다 해야 되니까 놀러 못 가요.
examples.en: I have to finish all my homework, so I cannot go out to play.
To take the exam, you have to bring an ID.

examples.ko: 약은 식사 후에 먹어야 되는데 깜빡했어요.
examples.en: I had to take the medicine after the meal, but I forgot.

examples.ko: 이 서류는 내일까지 내야 되고 저 서류는 다음 주까지 내면 돼요.
examples.en: This document has to be handed in by tomorrow, and that one is fine by next week.

compare.difference: The two are near-synonyms. “-어야 되다” is more spoken and “-어야 하다” more formal.
“-어야” alone is a condition (“only if”); “-어야 되다” is the obligation.

pair.en: You pass only if you study.

pitfalls.note: The spoken form is “돼요”, not “되요”.
A ㅂ-irregular adjective turns ㅂ into “우”.
pitfalls.en: The problem has to be easy.

topik_tip: “-어야 되다 / -어야 하다” (have to) and “-으면 안 되다” (must not) are the matching pair.

label: not (negation)
meaning_en: The long negation of verbs and adjectives: “-지 않다” means “do not, is not”. It is neutral and fits both speech and writing, and it is the counterpart of the short “안 + verb”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems with no change (“가다 → 가지 않다”, “예쁘다 → 예쁘지 않다”, “춥다 → 춥지 않다”), and the tense goes on “않다” (“가지 않았다, 가지 않을 거예요”). For a noun with “이다” the negation is “이/가 아니다”. With a “하다” verb the short form is “공부 안 해요”, not “안 공부해요”. It does not form commands or suggestions: those are “-지 마세요” and “-지 맙시다”. “-지 않아도 되다” means “do not have to”, and “-지 않으면 안 되다” means “must”.

examples.en: I do not eat meat.
The weather is not cold today.
I did not go to school yesterday.

examples.ko: 이 음식은 맵지 않으니까 드셔 보세요.
examples.en: This food is not spicy, so please try it.
You do not have to hurry.

compare.difference: “안” and “-지 않다” are near-synonyms. “안” is shorter and more spoken; “-지 않다” suits writing too.
“-지 않다” says one does not (by choice or fact); “-지 못하다” says one cannot.

pair.en: I do not go to school.

pitfalls.note: A noun with “이다” is negated with “이/가 아니다”.
The tense goes on “않다”, not on the first verb.
pitfalls.en: I did not go to school.

topik_tip: “안 + verb” and “-지 않다” are the two ways to negate; “못” and “-지 못하다” mean cannot.

label: can, be able to
meaning_en: An expression for ability, possibility and, in some contexts, permission: “can X, be able to X, it is possible that X”. The negative “-ㄹ 수 없다” means “cannot”.
usage: After a vowel or ㄹ it is “-ㄹ 수 있다”, after other consonants “-을 수 있다”: “읽다 → 읽을 수 있다”, “가다 → 갈 수 있다”, “놀다 → 놀 수 있다” and “만들다 → 만들 수 있다” (the ㄹ stays), “듣다 → 들을 수 있다”, “눕다 → 누울 수 있다”. With “이다” and adjectives it is a possibility (“학생일 수 있다”, “어려울 수 있다”). “-ㄹ 수도 있다” means “might”. “수” is a separate word, written with a space. Permission can be asked and given with it in formal signs (“사진을 찍을 수 있습니다”). The opposite is “-ㄹ 수 없다”.

examples.en: I can read Korean.
Can you sing this song?

examples.ko: 내일은 시간이 없어서 갈 수 없어요.
examples.en: I have no time tomorrow, so I cannot go.

examples.ko: 저는 매운 음식을 먹을 수 없어요.
examples.en: I cannot eat spicy food.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 거짓말을 할 수도 있어요.
examples.en: It is possible that person is lying.
You can take photos here.

compare.difference: “-ㄹ 수 없다” and “-지 못하다” are near-synonyms for cannot. “-ㄹ 수 없다” is a little more formal.
“-ㄹ 수 있다” says something is possible or doable; “-어도 되다” says it is allowed.

pitfalls.note: “수” is a separate word, spaced from the modifier and from “있다”.
A ㄹ-stem merges the ㄹ with “-ㄹ”.

topik_tip: Ability is “-ㄹ 수 있다”; “-ㄹ 수밖에 없다” (no choice but) is a different pattern.

label: cannot (circumstances)
meaning_en: An expression for inability: “cannot X, was unable to X”. It says that the action does not happen because of a lack of ability or because of circumstances, not by choice.
usage: It attaches to verb stems with no change: “먹다 → 먹지 못하다”, “가다 → 가지 못하다”, “쓰다 → 쓰지 못하다”; the tense goes on “못하다” (“못했다, 못해요”). The short form is “못 + verb” (“못 가요”), written with a space. “못하다” without a space (“노래를 못하다”) means “be bad at”. It is a little more formal than “못”. In writing “-지 못하고” (unable to ... and) and “-지 못한 채” are frequent. The matching expression of choice is “-지 않다”.

examples.ko: 어제는 너무 바빠서 점심도 먹지 못하고 일만 했어요.
examples.en: I was so busy yesterday that I worked without even eating lunch.

examples.ko: 감기에 걸려서 학교에 가지 못한다고 전화했어요.
examples.en: I called to say that I could not go to school because of a cold.

examples.ko: 아직 한국어로 편지를 쓰지 못하는 학생도 있어요.
examples.en: There are students who still cannot write letters in Korean.

examples.ko: 그 소식을 듣고 기쁨을 감추지 못하였다.
examples.en: On hearing the news, they could not hide their joy.
It was noisy, so I could not sleep.

compare.difference: “-지 않다” is a denial of fact or a choice; “-지 못하다” is inability.
“못 하다” (spaced) is “cannot do it now”; “못하다” (together) is “be bad at it”.

pair.ko: 오늘은 목이 아파서 노래를 못 해요.
pair.en: Today my throat hurts, so I cannot sing.

pitfalls.note: The tense goes on “못하다”.
In the short form, “못” is a separate word.

topik_tip: Spacing contrast to know: “못 하다” (cannot) versus “못하다” (bad at).

label: before doing
meaning_en: An expression for “before X happens”: “먹기 전에” (before eating), “자기 전에” (before going to bed). It places the main clause earlier than the clause with “-기”. With a noun it is “N 전에” (“식사 전에, 일주일 전에”).
usage: It attaches to verb stems with no tense ending, even when the main clause is in the past: “먹다 → 먹기 전에”, “자다 → 자기 전에”, “오다 → 오기 전에”, “만들다 → 만들기 전에” (the ㄹ stays). The main clause may be a command, a plan or a past event. A noun of duration plus “전에” means “ago” (“일 년 전에”). Without a clause “전에” alone means “before, previously” (“전에 만난 적이 있다”). The opposite is “-은 후에”.

examples.en: Brush your teeth before you go to bed.
I learned Korean before coming to Korea.
I wash my hands before eating.

examples.ko: 수업이 시작하기 전에 교실에 도착해야 합니다.
examples.en: You have to arrive in the classroom before class starts.

examples.ko: 일 년 전에 이 집으로 이사했어요.
examples.en: I moved to this house a year ago.

compare.difference: The two are opposites: “-기 전에” is before, “-은 후에” is after.

pitfalls.note: The first verb never takes the past tense.
pitfalls.en: I washed my hands before eating.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ before “-기”.
pitfalls.en: I bought the ingredients before making the cake.

topik_tip: The verb before “전에” stays in the plain “-기” form whatever the tense of the sentence.

label: after doing
meaning_en: An expression for “after X is done”: “먹은 후에” (after eating), “졸업한 후에” (after graduating). It places the main clause later than the clause with “-은 후에”. With a noun it is “N 후에” (“식사 후에, 삼 일 후에”).
usage: It attaches to verb stems with the past modifier: after a vowel “-ㄴ”, after a consonant “-은”: “가다 → 간 후에”, “먹다 → 먹은 후에”, “끝나다 → 끝난 후에”, “만들다 → 만든 후에” (the ㄹ drops). “후” is a separate word. “-은 뒤에” is a near-synonym and so is “-고 나서”. The noun form is “N 후에”: “삼 일 후에” (in three days), “식사 후에”. A short form “-ㄴ 후” (without “에”) is used in writing.

examples.en: Take the medicine after you eat.
After graduating from university, I joined a company.

examples.ko: 수업이 끝난 후에 같이 점심 먹을까요?
examples.en: Shall we have lunch together after class ends?
Please come again in three days.

examples.ko: 운동한 후에는 물을 많이 마셔야 해요.
examples.en: After exercising, you should drink plenty of water.

compare.difference: The two are opposites: “-은 후에” is after, “-기 전에” is before.
“-은 후에” and “-은 뒤에” are near-synonyms.

pitfalls.note: The first verb takes the past modifier, not the present.
pitfalls.en: Take the medicine after you eat.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem drops the ㄹ before “-ㄴ”.
pitfalls.en: After making the cake, I packaged it.

topik_tip: “-은 후에 / -은 뒤에 / -고 나서” are interchangeable in most simple sentences.
